description_en: This rectangular three-bayed Phalcā is open on three sides and attached to the houses behind it. Situated in Cyāsal, it stands to the east of the three-headed Gaṇeśa shrine and north-east of Nhugu Phalcā (LAL4159). In 2019, it was almost entirely demolished and reconstructed using new materials (for the carved pillars, beams, etc.). It had been in a dilapidated state since the 2015 earthquakes and had suffered major water damage.Atāḥ Phalcā is predominantly used by women, whereas the Phalcā opposite is sometimes referred to as Nhugu (male) Phalcā due to a similarly gendered division in its use.Dāphā bhajansare also performed there. The Cyāsal Byan͂jankāra Dāphā Khalaḥ performsdāphā bhajanin the Phalcā on the day of Indrajātrā.This Phalcā is particularly important due to the role it plays in the social and ritual life of the neighbourhood.
description_ne: च्यासलमा रहेको यो तीनतले चारकुने फल्चा तीन तिर खुला छ, पछाडिपट्टि पूर्वी दिशामा तीनटाउके गणेशको मन्दिरसँग र उत्तरपूर्वमा न्हुगु फल्चा (LAL4159) सँग जोडिएको छ । यो अताः फल्चा विशेष गरी आइमाई मानिसहरूले प्रयोग गर्ने गर्दछन्, यसको सामुन्ने रहेको फल्चालाई यदाकदा न्हुगु (लोग्नेमान्छे) फल्चा भन्ने गरिएको पाइन्छ । यस फल्चामा दापा भजनहरू पनि गर्ने गरिन्छ । जस्तै इन्द्रजात्राको दिन च्यासल व्यञ्जनकार दापा खलःले यस फल्चामा भजन गाउने गर्दछ ।
monument_assessment: Rebuilt, Demolition/Dismantling, Heavily damaged (collapsed, demolished, major cracks and structural damages)

historical_events.event_description: Atāḥ Phalcā was part of the first PhotoKathmandu festival, which included an exhibition and curated walk entitled 'Patis in Patan'. It was curated by Sujan Chitrakar (Kathmandu University, Centre for Art & Design), Rajendra Shakya (South Asia Institute branch office, Heidelberg) and Christiane Brosius (Heidelberg Centre for Transcultural Studies, HCTS) in November 2015 following the 2015 earthquakes. The project focused on the everyday lives of people in public spaces such as the arcaded rest houses. Photographs were taken of elderly women using the Phalcā, who also spoke with interviewees about their lives and the role of the Phalcā in them. A selection of these photographs was exhibited on the walls inside the building and next to it.The Phalcā has been used as an exhibition space to tell the stories of the women who sit in it every day, and to create awareness of and interest in the site as a social space.

The Phalcā was reconstructed almost entirely without using older materials. It is an important site for the community, but had been in a badly damaged state due to water leakage and the earthquakes of 2015.

Before its reconstruction in 2019, a metal plate dated NS 842 could be seen on the beam of the Phalcā.However, it did not state what happened on that date. The metal plate was removed during the reconstruction.
